title: Not seen by marks (section 5)
hookLine: can the Tathagata be known by bodily marks? no; where there are marks there is illusion

lines: THE MARKS OF A GREAT BEING.
IS THAT HOW YOU KNOW ONE?
cards: A bronze Buddha sits behind museum glass. A rounded swell on the crown of the head, long earlobes, hair in small tight curls, a calm face with eyes half closed.

Some of those features echo a list Buddhist tradition keeps: the marks of a great being, signs said to appear on the body of a Buddha. So here's a fair question. If a Buddha has marks, is that how you recognize one?
Section five of the Diamond Sutra asks exactly that, and the Buddha is the one asking.

teach.h: CAN HE BE SEEN BY HIS MARKS?
teach.b: First, the question. The Buddha asks Subhuti: can the Tathagata be seen by means of his bodily marks? Tathagata is the name the Buddha uses for himself in the sutras.
It's a test, and Subhuti doesn't take the easy answer. Second, the answer. No, Subhuti says, because the marks the Tathagata spoke of are no marks.
The marks are named, and in the same breath they're said not to be what they seem. This sutra will do that again and again. Third, the line the section turns on.

teach.h: NO: THE MARKS ARE NO MARKS.
teach.b: The Buddha agrees, and goes further: wherever there are marks, there is illusion; when you see that marks are no marks, you see the Tathagata.
That's a paraphrase; the sutra's own words are short and strange, and translators put them differently. The point isn't that the statue is a lie, or that the body didn't matter.
The sutra doesn't ask anyone to throw the statue out. It asks what you think you're seeing when you look at it.
Fourth, the marks of a day.
A uniform, an accent, a car, a job title, a wheelchair, a tattoo: each gets sorted in half a second.

The sorting is useful. It's also, this sutra says, where the illusion starts, because the person never fits inside the mark. And the first picture the Diamond Sutra cuts through is the picture of the Buddha himself.

how: In Mahayana communities the Diamond Sutra is chanted, copied and studied, and a short passage like this one is often read slowly and talked over with a teacher.

games.q: what does “not seen by marks” mean?
o: only statues show the true marks of the Buddha
the Buddha isn't truly known by his body's special signs
the Buddha's body had no special signs at all

p: can he be seen by bodily marks?
no: the marks are no marks

s: in section five, Subhuti says the Tathagata can't be seen by bodily marks
the marks the Tathagata spoke of, he says, are no marks.
the Diamond Sutra says the Buddha's body had no special signs
it speaks of the marks; it says he isn't known by them.
this section tells people to throw away Buddha images
it doesn't ask anyone to throw the statue out. it asks what you think you're seeing.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks whether the Tathagata can be seen by his bodily marks. what do you answer?
o: yes: the marks are how a Buddha is known.
no: the marks he spoke of are no marks.
it depends on how good the statue is.
games.why: Subhuti says no, and the Buddha goes further: wherever there are marks, there is illusion; see marks as no marks, and you see the Tathagata.

practice: Bring to mind someone you know mostly by a mark: the neighbor with the loud truck, the coworker with the sharp voice, the cashier in the green vest.
Name each mark on an out-breath and set it down, then stay with what's left: someone who wakes up, gets tired, has a mother or had one, hopes the day goes well.
When the marks come back, let them, and look a little longer than half a second.

wordCard.voice: Not seen by marks. The Buddha isn't known by the body's signs; where there are marks, the sutra says, there is illusion. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a mark or sign; the word for the body's marks of a great being.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond the marks. Even the Buddha isn't seen by them. See you tomorrow.
